part: ESP32-WROOM-32 development board ("DevKit"), classic 30-pin, headers already soldered
check_before_buying: Module marking says WROOM-32 (not WROVER); pins labelled GPIO16/17/18/23/26/27/33/14; a USB data port. Do not substitute an ESP32-C3, ESP32-S3 or a WROVER board without re-checking every pin and the firmware — GPIO16/17 are used for PSRAM on WROVER.
5 V part with 4-pin header VCC/TRIG/ECHO/GND; four corner mounting holes (the sensor head expects them — SR04_HOLE_X/Y in the CAD are VERIFY values).

part: SG90-size positional micro servo with its factory double-arm horn
check_before_buying: 180°-type positional servo, not continuous-rotation ("360°") — those cannot hold an angle. Keep the factory horn and spline.
Pins VCC/GND/DIN/CLK/CS/DC/RST/BL; board 56.5 × 34 mm (check your revision).

part: DFRobot DFR1026 charge/discharge module (5 V / 2 A output)
check_before_buying: Accepts 4.6–5.4 V input, ~2 A charge. It has no USB connector — needs E6. See the open issue before committing to it.

part: USB-C female power-input breakout with 5.1 kΩ pull-downs on both CC1 and CC2
check_before_buying: The two 5.1 kΩ resistors (one per CC pin) are what make a USB-C charger switch on 5 V. No Power Delivery (PD) trigger board — this project must never receive 9 V or 12 V.

Protected (built-in protection circuit). Check the datasheet for ≥2.1 A charge and ≥3 A continuous discharge — capacity alone is not enough. Buy from a reputable supplier; protected cells are slightly longer than bare ones, so check the holder fits.
reference_candidate: Any reputable protected 18650 meeting both current ratings

check_before_buying: Flying leads (no soldering to the cell), fits a protected cell's length.

part: 12 mm latching push-on/push-off button, 2 terminals, single-pole single-throw (SPST)
check_before_buying: Rated ≥2 A at 5 V DC (check the DC rating, not only the AC one). Panel hole 12 mm; fascia is 2.6 mm thick.
reference_candidate: Generic 12 mm latching metal push button

check_before_buying: On battery positive, as close to the holder as practical. Blade (ATM/mini) or 5 × 20 mm glass both fine.

part: 1000 µF electrolytic capacitor, ≥10 V (16 V gives margin)
check_before_buying: Polarised: stripe = negative. Mounted at the servo end of its supply branch.
ECHO divider R1.
ECHO divider R2.

part: Jumper leads, mostly female–female, plus short 22–24 AWG stranded power wire
check_before_buying: Power branches (charger → switch → load) in 22 AWG; signal leads can be jumpers.
reference_candidate: Assorted Dupont leads + 22 AWG silicone wire

check_before_buying: Polarised so it cannot be reversed (for example JST-XH 2.54 mm). Lets the ESP32's power lead unplug for programming.

part: Heat-shrink, double-sided foam tape, 2 battery straps or zip ties (≤3.6 mm wide), 4 rubber feet
check_before_buying: Straps go round the holder, not the bare cell.

part: 5 V / 3 A USB-C wall supply + USB-C cable
check_before_buying: Plain 5 V is enough; a PD charger also works because the breakout only asks for 5 V.
reference_candidate: Any reputable 5 V 3 A USB-C supply

part: USB data cable for the ESP32 board
check_before_buying: Micro-USB or USB-C to match E1. Charge-only cables will not program.
257 g is the solid-volume upper bound for all required parts plus the coupon (from cad/geometry_report.json); your slicer's figure with walls + infill will be lower.

part: 3.3 V-logic USB-to-serial adapter + 2 female jumper leads
check_before_buying: Only for the live console. CP2102, CH340 or FT232 type, voltage set to 3.3 V. Only its RX and GND are used; VCC stays unconnected. See LIVE_LINK.md.
